prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at magic twist angles and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opening moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep B028 alone as the whole prize, with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. The reasons are scientific and have not changed. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted a collapse of the bandwidth at a specific twist angle from a simple starting point, and the 2018 experiments found correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle. Many independent groups have since reproduced the phases and extended them to a family of moire systems in which interaction strength is tuned by angle and gate rather than by chemistry. That is a controllable arena for strongly correlated many-body physics, which is why I judge it the discovery of a platform and not of a single material. The round has also sharpened what the citation should say: it should be worded around flat bands and correlated phases, not around the mechanism of the superconductivity. My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1; what changed is that I now regard B022 as better argued than I first allowed, and I say so below.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains timing: the experiments date from 2018, the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators are debated, and the boundary between the founding result and later moire work (Dean and Young groups, fractional Chern insulators) is not sharp. I treat this as a real risk. Attribution is imperfect as well: Cao and the first-author team are outside three names, and Bistritzer's share relative to MacDonald is a judgement call; I keep him because the 2011 paper is the one that made the quantitative magic-angle prediction. If the committee concludes that a prize should wait until the mechanism is understood, B022 is the candidate I would move to, because it is mature and cleanly attributed, even though I still consider it narrower in conceptual novelty.

responses.point: Kroll holds B022 (Katori, Ye) as a whole prize, arguing that the magic-wavelength lattice is a clear concept turned into 10^-18 performance that is independently reproduced, and that the 2005 and 2012 overlap is the main counterargument.
responses.response: The chair asks whether B022 is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. Lindroth's reply that no earlier prize gave a way to interrogate many neutral atoms at once at this precision persuades me that it is not a third helping of the same thing, and I withdraw part of my round-1 framing of it as more technological than conceptual. I still weigh B028 higher for the new class of many-body phenomena, but I now regard that as a difference of judgement about conceptual breadth, not a disqualification of B022. I keep B022 as my first alternative and would support it if B028 is judged premature.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that Katori's state-insensitive lattice is an idea about atomic structure and light shifts and not just engineering, and that B003 has a sharper overlap problem with Parisi than B022 has with earlier prizes.
responses.response: She is right on both points, and I move accordingly. On the first, I concede the conceptual step is real. On the second, the cavity method's foundations lie substantially with Parisi and the replica tradition, which makes B003 harder to credit to Mezard and Zecchina alone, and I cannot resolve the boundary from the text supplied. That is why B003, my own opening first choice, no longer appears among my alternatives; it is replaced by B048, which has a more settled interpretation and a three-name credit I can defend.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B014 to B028 for timing and independence reasons, would resist citing the superconductivity as the achievement, and reads the open mechanism as a reason to word the citation around flat bands and correlated phases.
responses.response: I agree, and my citation is worded that way: the prediction of flat bands and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which are observed phenomena and not a claim about their origin. His disclosure about circuit QED explains why B014 is not in his configuration, and I see no reason to reopen it. Where I differ is only emphasis: he treats the unsettled mechanism mainly as a matter of wording, whereas I also treat it as a residual maturity risk that the committee should record openly.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, prefers B002 (Halzen alone) with B022, and says the pairing depends on B002 being able to carry a half of a prize; if it cannot, B037 or B028 is the better partner for B022.
responses.response: A B002 plus B022 prize would be two clean and independent measurement-driven discoveries, but I cannot support B002 without a principle that makes one name the decisive credit for a collaboration of hundreds, and the chair himself flags that as the weak point and notes that AMANDA-era people are outside the credit. I also note that B028 plus B022 would need five names, which the three-person limit rules out. I therefore see B028 alone and B022 alone as the two coherent single-theme configurations, and the B002 pairing as the one I find hardest to defend on credit.

responses.point: Danielsson has set aside B037 as a first choice because the committee lacks a principle for crediting detector architects, and prefers the B002 plus B022 pairing because it uses exactly three names with well-defined credit.
responses.response: His reasoning on B037 is the one I raised in round 1, and I respect that he followed it through even though he still regards the Higgs experimental discovery as the most fundamental result. I do not think B002's credit is as well defined as he does: his own case against names the AMANDA colleagues and the incomplete source identification. For that reason I would not follow him to the pairing, but I agree that if the committee wants two distinct parts, B022 is the strongest component on the list.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the pairing mechanism is not the discovery being recognised and that the Dean-group work belongs to the later field and not to the founding discovery; he would not wait a decade for the mechanism.
responses.response: I agree with the first part and with his reading of the Dean group, and I rely on it for the three-name allocation. I am less comfortable with dismissing the cost of waiting for the mechanism entirely: if the field is still revising its account of the correlated states, the downside of an early prize is a citation that reads as dated. That is why I keep a mature alternative, B022, and not only a second moire-adjacent one.

uncertainties: Whether the unresolved origin of the superconductivity makes the prize premature, or whether a citation limited to flat bands and correlated phases is enough
Whether Bistritzer belongs with MacDonald, and whether a three-name limit properly reflects the experimental side given Cao and the first-author team
Whether the committee would prefer B022 alone as the mature and cleanly attributed option this year
My judgement of B022 and B048 is that of someone outside precision metrology and topological materials, and I defer partly to the specialists on both
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My neural-network and statistical-physics work is adjacent to B003, which I opened with but no longer prefer, and I have no documented tie to the credited names of B028, B022 or B048. I do not work on moire materials, optical clocks or topological insulators.
